title: Hub can identify the homeowner through account-registration data
description: During registration and device enrollment, the Home Hub receives direct identifiers and account attributes (e.g., email, username, phone number, household details, device ownership bindings). This enables the hub/system to identify a natural person and associate enrolled cameras/sensors with that homeowner.
assumptions: Registration involves at least one persistent account identifier and binds devices to that account.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN Pro identifyability concepts; the exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree edition.

title: Account and device-enrollment data can link multiple devices and actions to one homeowner
description: The registration flow lets the Home Hub correlate the homeowner's account with multiple cameras/sensors being enrolled. This creates a stable linkage between person, household, and device set, making later events from those devices linkable to the same data subject.
assumptions: The hub maintains a persistent account or household identifier across enrolled devices.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is an informed approximation for linkability at the receiving process and flow.

title: Registration and enrollment disclose sensitive household and device information
description: The flow may disclose personal and context-rich data to the Home Hub, such as account credentials or contact details, home occupancy patterns inferred from device types/placement, and the existence/location of cameras and sensors in the home. Such disclosure exceeds bare connectivity metadata and reveals private household characteristics.
assumptions: Enrollment transmits device metadata such as model, location/room label, capabilities, or serial numbers.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; disclosure clearly applies but sub-node naming may differ across versions.

title: Homeowner may be unable to deny having registered or enrolled specific devices
description: If the Home Hub records account creation and device-enrollment events together with persistent identifiers, timestamps, and device serials, the resulting evidence may allow the system operator to prove that the homeowner performed these actions. This undermines plausible deniability for participation in setup and ownership binding.
assumptions: The hub or backend keeps logs of registration and enrollment operations.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is included because setup flows commonly generate durable audit/log evidence, but applicability depends on actual logging design.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of how registration data and enrolled-device metadata will be used
description: At account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may not have sufficient visibility into how the Home Hub or associated services will process identifiers, device metadata, and household configuration data, including whether the data will support analytics, remote management, sharing, or retention beyond setup.
assumptions: The flow or interface does not fully explain downstream processing purposes, retention, or sharing.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the transparency of notices and UI presented during registration.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more personal data than necessary or without valid consent/legal basis
description: The setup flow may request or transmit excessive identifiers, household details, or device metadata for the purpose of creating an account and pairing devices. If the homeowner is not given a genuine choice or the collection is broader than necessary for setup, the flow risks non-compliance with data minimization, purpose limitation, and consent/legal-basis requirements.
assumptions: The design may require optional profile fields or transmit detailed device/household metadata by default.
uncertainty_note: Compliance threats are context- and jurisdiction-dependent; exact obligations vary.

title: Temporary access code can reveal guest identity or relationship
description: The temporary access code entered by the guest may be associated by the Home Hub with a specific guest invitation, booking, or household event. Processing this code on the Home Hub can therefore identify the guest directly or indirectly, or reveal their relationship to the household, beyond the minimum needed to unlock the door.
assumptions: The code is unique per guest, visit, or invitation and the Home Hub can map it to a specific person or small group.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for identifiability from authentication data; exact subtree citation was not present in the retrieved context.

title: Door-unlock attempt can disclose guest participation or presence
description: Observation of this flow or the Home Hub's immediate behavior in response to the entered temporary code may allow an observer to infer that a guest is currently present at, or attempting to access, the home. This reveals data-subject involvement without needing to read the code itself.
assumptions: An attacker can observe the communication, keypad use, timing, status lights, sounds, or unlock response at the Home Hub.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is inferred from general detecting threats via observed communication/side-effects, consistent with the retrieved methodology excerpt.

title: Temporary code entry may disclose sensitive household activity patterns
description: Use of a guest temporary access code can reveal sensitive information such as that the occupants are hosting visitors, renting out the property, or granting access to a particular category of person at a particular time. Even if the code itself is protected, the event and its context may disclose private household routines or circumstances.
assumptions: The mere existence, timing, or frequency of guest-code use is observable or logged and can be correlated with household activities.
uncertainty_note: Sensitive-data-disclosure applicability depends on context; if guest access is routine and not sensitive in this deployment, this threat may be lower relevance. Tree-node id is best-effort.

title: Guest may be unaware how temporary code use is processed and logged
description: When entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub, the guest may not be adequately informed that the code use can be logged, linked to time and location, and potentially associated with their visit. This creates a privacy threat from insufficient transparency about collection and processing on this flow.
assumptions: The system records code-entry events or otherwise processes them beyond the immediate unlock decision, and the guest is not clearly informed at the point of entry.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on general unawareness/lack-of-transparency reasoning; exact subtree citation not available in the retrieved context.

title: Guest may have no meaningful choice or consent regarding processing of access-code data
description: To gain entry, the guest may be forced to submit the temporary code to the Home Hub without any practical ability to refuse associated logging, profiling, or retention of the access event. This can undermine freely given consent or user control over personal data processing tied to the visit.
assumptions: Access-code submission is mandatory for entry and the system performs secondary privacy-relevant processing such as storage, correlation, or analytics.
uncertainty_note: This applies only if consent or user choice is the intended legal/control basis for this processing; otherwise non-compliance may be a weaker fit. Tree-node id is best-effort.

title: Local event history enables behaviour linkage
description: Writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a persistent local event log creates a time-series that can be linked into patterns about household routines, occupancy, arrivals/departures, and activity sequences. Even if single events seem harmless, the stored log can link multiple observations to the same home or residents over time.
assumptions: The log retains event records with timestamps and device or zone identifiers long enough to reconstruct activity patterns.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement; retrieved context confirms L applies to Process->DataStore flows but did not provide the exact subtree for linkability.

title: Logged sensor events can identify residents or household presence
description: The local event log may reveal who is at home, when occupants wake, leave, return, or move through rooms. If events are associated with specific sensors, rooms, devices, or user accounts, the stored records can identify individuals or at minimum the household's presence and habits.
assumptions: Events are timestamped and associated with particular sensors, locations, or accounts; the log is accessible to someone able to inspect it later.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiability depends on event granularity and whether sensor/location metadata is stored.

title: Retained event log reduces residents' ability to deny actions or presence
description: Persisting sensor events creates retained evidence that a door opened, motion occurred, or a sensor was triggered at a certain time. This evidence can later be used to dispute a resident's denial of being present, moving in a room, or opening an entry point.
assumptions: The event log is persistent and considered sufficiently trustworthy by whoever relies on it.

title: Local event log discloses intimate household activities
description: Motion and door events recorded over time can disclose sensitive private facts such as sleep schedules, periods of absence, room usage, visitor activity, and daily routines. A local log that preserves raw events increases the amount of private household information available for later inspection.
assumptions: The datastore stores raw or only lightly processed event data with timestamps.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate; disclosure clearly applies for this flow but the exact subtree was not supplied in retrieved context.

title: Residents may be unaware that detailed in-home events are being persisted
description: If the Home Hub silently writes sensor events to a local datastore, residents or guests may not realize that detailed records of movements and door activity are retained. This lack of awareness undermines predictability and users' ability to understand what personal data is stored.
assumptions: The system does not provide clear notice or indicators about local event logging and retention.
uncertainty_note: Exact detectability subtree is based on best judgement.

title: Local logging may be unawared or unexpected by data subjects
description: People in the home, especially guests or secondary residents, may be unaware that motion and door sensor triggers are being written into a local event log. They may not understand the extent, retention, or possible later use of these records.
assumptions: Users/visitors are not explicitly informed about event logging, or the notice is insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate; this is grounded in unawareness of collection/storage for the flow.

title: Persistent event logging may exceed consent or expected purpose
description: Recording all motion, door, and sensor events into a local log may go beyond what residents, guests, or other data subjects consented to or reasonably expect, especially if data is kept longer than necessary or used for secondary purposes such as monitoring behaviour.
assumptions: Consent, legitimate expectation, or purpose limitation for detailed event retention has not been clearly established.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance subtree is approximate because applicable legal/policy obligations are system-specific.

title: Video clips may be uploaded to cloud storage without adequate transmission protection
description: Recorded camera clips contain highly sensitive personal data. If the Home Hub uploads them over an insecure or weakly authenticated channel, unauthorized parties could intercept or gain access to the clips during transfer or via overly broad storage access on the receiving side, resulting in disclosure beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the upload path or receiving cloud endpoint may lack strong transport security, endpoint authentication, or least-privilege access controls.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved context explicitly supports Dd.4.2 for accessibility/broad access of data; applying it to this upload flow is a best-judgment mapping because the exact subtree for disclosure during transfer was not provided in the retrieved snippets.

title: Users may be unaware that recorded clips are uploaded to cloud storage
description: If the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips to the cloud without clear visibility or understandable notice, data subjects may not realize remote storage occurs, for how long clips are retained, or who can access them. This undermines predictability and informed user expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the system may not provide sufficiently prominent indicators, explanations, or settings around cloud upload behavior.
uncertainty_note: Threat clearly fits Unawareness for this flow, but the exact tree node id is based on best judgment because the relevant Unawareness subtree was not included in the retrieved context.

title: Uploading camera clips to the cloud may occur without a valid legal basis or exceed stated purpose
description: Sending recorded home camera footage to cloud video storage may process more personal data than necessary, retain it longer than justified, or transfer it for purposes not covered by the user's consent, contract, or other legal basis. This creates non-compliance with data minimization, purpose limitation, retention, and transparency obligations.
assumptions: Assumes cloud upload is optional or broader than strictly necessary for the core service, or that retention/purpose constraints are not clearly enforced.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance is plausible for this flow, but the exact node id is best-judgment because no Nc threat-tree nodes were provided in the retrieved context.

title: Lack of upload evidence could allow repudiation of clip transfers
description: If the system does not maintain reliable, tamper-evident records of when the Home Hub uploaded specific clips to cloud storage, the operator or user may be unable to prove that a given transfer occurred, what data was sent, or under which settings and authorization. This weakens accountability for privacy-relevant processing.
assumptions: Assumes upload events, consent state, and retention-policy decisions are not robustly logged or auditable.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation is a genuine accountability/privacy concern for this flow, but the exact Nr node id is inferred rather than taken from retrieved context.

title: Stored cloud video clips can enable linkage across time, devices, or household members
description: Once clips are centralized in cloud storage, metadata such as account identifiers, device IDs, timestamps, locations, and recurring patterns can link multiple recordings to the same household or individuals. This increases the ability to correlate behavior over time and across services.
assumptions: Assumes cloud storage preserves or can associate clip metadata across uploads and possibly across related services/accounts.
uncertainty_note: Linkability is a credible threat for centralized video storage, but the exact node id is best-judgment because no Linkability subtree details were retrieved.

title: Cloud-stored video clips may enable identification of residents or visitors
description: Video footage stored in the cloud can directly reveal faces, voices, clothing, routines, and home interiors. Even if clips are referenced indirectly, associated metadata and visual content may make it possible to identify specific residents, visitors, or neighbors.
assumptions: Assumes uploaded clips contain people or contextual information sufficient for recognition or re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Identification is strongly applicable to video storage, but the exact tree node id is based on best judgment due to lack of retrieved Identification nodes.

title: Unnecessary disclosure of detailed motion-event data to backend
description: The Home Hub forwards a real-time motion alert to the mobile app backend across a process boundary. If the alert contains more personal data than strictly needed for notification handling—such as exact timestamps, device identifiers, room/location labels, continuous event frequency, or raw sensor context—this creates avoidable explicit data disclosure. Motion alerts can reveal occupant presence patterns and behavior, so only the minimum fields required for backend processing should be sent.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert contains personal or household behavioral data and that some included fields may be unnecessary for the backend's purpose.

title: Implicit disclosure of occupancy patterns through motion-alert metadata
description: Even if the payload is limited to a simple motion event, repeated real-time alerts sent from the Home Hub to the backend can implicitly disclose sensitive household patterns such as when people are home, sleeping, away, or moving between spaces. Timing, frequency, and source metadata may therefore reveal personal information beyond the explicit alert content.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can observe alert timing/frequency and associate alerts with a specific household or device.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best judgment for implicit/metadata-based disclosure; exact subnode naming may vary across LINDDUN Pro threat-tree versions.

title: Linkability of motion alerts to a specific household or user account
description: If the backend receives persistent hub identifiers, account identifiers, or stable pseudonyms together with each motion alert, separate events can be linked over time to the same household or user. This enables construction of detailed behavioral profiles from multiple alerts, increasing privacy risk beyond the individual event.
assumptions: Assumes stable identifiers or otherwise consistent attributes accompany the alert and are visible at the backend.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgment; retrieved context did not include the applicable Linking subtree details.

title: Identifiability of residents from motion-alert contents or identifiers
description: A real-time motion alert may allow the backend to identify the household or infer the identity of residents when combined with account data, exact device identifiers, address-linked installation records, or uniquely patterned activity. This turns what might seem like sensor telemetry into identifiable personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the backend has access to subscriber/account information or other auxiliary data enabling re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected using general LINDDUN knowledge; exact subnode may differ in a specific LINDDUN Pro tree release.

title: Detectability of in-home activity from presence of motion-alert traffic
description: The mere arrival of a motion alert at the backend can make the occurrence of in-home activity detectable, even before considering full content. Backend-side observability of these events may allow operators or connected components to detect when motion occurred at a household, exposing sensitive facts such as presence at home.
assumptions: Assumes the backend or adjacent monitoring components can observe message occurrence and timing.
uncertainty_note: Applicable detectability threat is plausible for event-presence signaling, but exact subtree node is based on best judgment due to missing mapping/tree details.

title: Notification content may disclose personal activity to unintended viewers
description: A pushed motion-detected notification can reveal that motion occurred at the homeowner's property and potentially when they are away or active. If notification text is shown on the lock screen, wearable, shared device, or preview banner, personal household activity data may be disclosed beyond the intended recipient. The flow should minimize content and avoid exposing precise event details unless necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification contains human-readable event details such as 'Motion detected at front door' and may be displayed in previews outside the app.

title: Repeated motion alerts can enable linkage of homeowner behavior patterns
description: Over time, motion-detected push notifications can be correlated to infer occupancy schedules, routines, sleep patterns, or travel periods of the homeowner/household. Even if each alert seems innocuous, the sequence and timing of notifications may make the data subject's activities linkable across events.
assumptions: Assumes the recipient device or related notification ecosystem retains timestamps/history of alerts.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best-fit judgement for linkability via event correlation; exact node labeling may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Notification metadata can make homeowner presence or absence detectable
description: The existence, timing, and frequency of motion notifications can allow an observer with access to the phone screen, notification logs, or push-service metadata to detect whether activity is occurring at the home, indirectly revealing occupancy or absence. This is a detectability risk even if the full content is hidden.
assumptions: Assumes some notification metadata (arrival time, app sender, count/frequency) is observable outside the secure app context.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node may differ depending on whether the methodology separates content visibility from metadata observability.

title: Vague or missing notification context may leave the homeowner unaware of processing implications
description: If the motion alert does not clearly indicate why the notification was sent, what data triggered it, or what downstream processing/sharing may occur, the homeowner may be insufficiently informed about surveillance-related personal-data processing. Lack of transparency in this outgoing notification flow can undermine user awareness.
assumptions: Assumes the notification or supporting UX does not adequately explain the trigger source and processing context.
uncertainty_note: This applies only if the notification experience lacks accessible explanation elsewhere in the app; transparency may be handled outside this specific flow.

title: Shared analytics may be linkable across datasets or customers at the vendor
description: Even if the backend shares aggregated device-usage analytics, the combination of stable dimensions, cohort breakdowns, timestamps, app/version metadata, or tenant-specific identifiers can enable the analytics vendor to link this dataset to other submissions or external data, reconstructing persistent patterns about the same app population or segments over time.
assumptions: Assumes the transmitted analytics contain repeated structure, quasi-identifiers, or metadata that remain stable across uploads and are visible to the vendor.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; exact subtree may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version and the precise fields shared.

title: Aggregated analytics may still reveal identities or small groups
description: Aggregation does not inherently prevent identifiability. If the backend sends fine-grained cohorts, rare device characteristics, low-count segments, or detailed time/location/app-usage dimensions, the vendor may infer or single out specific users or very small groups.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style controls, or suppression for low-count cells are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Applies strongly when aggregates are granular or sparse; if robust privacy-preserving aggregation is used, this risk may be reduced.

title: Vendor processing may expose information beyond the original analytics purpose
description: Once the cloud analytics vendor receives the analytics, it may derive additional insights such as behavioral trends, performance issues tied to user segments, commercial intelligence, or inferred attributes not explicitly intended by the sending backend. This creates a detectability/disclosure risk at the receiving party.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor can inspect, profile, mine, or otherwise analyze the received analytics beyond simple storage/relay.
uncertainty_note: Exact distinction between disclosure and detectability depends on the project's interpretation of the LINDDUN Pro tree; node chosen by best judgement.

title: Further vendor-side use of analytics may be unexpected to users
description: Users may reasonably expect analytics to support app improvement within the service provider, but not necessarily onward sharing to a separate cloud analytics vendor that can process the data under its own operational model. This can make the processing and recipients insufficiently transparent from the data subject perspective.
assumptions: Assumes user-facing notices do not clearly explain this third-party analytics sharing and its implications.
uncertainty_note: This is strongest if privacy notices or in-app disclosures do not clearly identify the vendor and purpose.

title: Third-party analytics sharing may exceed consent or declared purpose
description: Sending device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor may be incompatible with the user's consent choices, enterprise commitments, or the originally declared purpose if the sharing is broader than necessary or not covered by a valid legal basis/contractual arrangement.
assumptions: Assumes either no valid opt-in/opt-out mechanism exists, consent is bundled/ambiguous, or the disclosed purpose did not clearly include this external sharing.
uncertainty_note: Compliance outcome depends on jurisdiction, contractual setup, and whether the analytics are truly anonymized versus merely aggregated.

title: Playback retrieval can expose a homeowner's presence patterns and private activities
description: When the backend retrieves stored video clips for playback, the returned footage may reveal identifiable occupants, visitors, routines, occupancy status, and activities inside or around the home. If the backend requests, handles, or returns broader footage than needed for the requested playback session, this increases the privacy impact of disclosure.
assumptions: Video clips contain personal data about residents or visitors and are retrievable by the backend for presentation to the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for disclosure of personal content during retrieval; exact sub-node may differ in the project's threat tree variant.

title: Retrieved video clips can be linked to a specific household or data subject
description: The backend's retrieval of stored clips can associate video content with an authenticated homeowner account, device identifiers, timestamps, camera identifiers, and household metadata. This enables linking the footage to a particular person or home, even when the clip itself might otherwise be less directly attributable.
assumptions: The backend has access to account, device, or camera metadata used to fetch and deliver the clip.
uncertainty_note: Exact D sub-node may vary depending on whether the project distinguishes identifiability from linkability at a finer granularity.

title: Backend may retrieve more video than necessary for the stated playback purpose
description: To serve playback, the backend might fetch full-resolution clips, adjacent time windows, or additional metadata beyond what is necessary for the homeowner's immediate request. Retrieving excess footage or metadata creates a risk of processing that is disproportionate to the playback purpose and therefore lacks adequate data minimization or purpose limitation.
assumptions: The retrieval operation could be implemented to fetch more content or metadata than strictly needed to play the requested clip.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine risk for retrieval flows, but the exact threat-tree node for unawareness/non-compliance around minimization may differ by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Video retrieval for playback may violate minimization, access-control, or retention obligations
description: The backend's handling of stored video for playback may be non-compliant if it retrieves clips without enforcing need-to-know access, uses footage for secondary purposes, or allows access to clips retained longer than permitted. Because the process receives and acts on the data, compliance failures materialize at the backend during retrieval.
assumptions: Applicable legal or policy obligations exist for residential video footage, including access control, purpose limitation, and retention constraints.
uncertainty_note: Exact compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and system policy; node id is a best-fit estimate.
